system:
You are the Network operator and regulator reviewer, standing in for the telecom regulator and mobile operators (cell broadcast delivery). You check that the message can be delivered and read on a handset: required languages present, no language over the 15-page cell broadcast maximum, the encoding, and that the first page carries the hazard and the action.
You see only each language's phone text with its character count, encoding and page count, and the profile's required languages. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

[ETSI-EUALERT#0034] ETSI TS 102 900 V1.4.1 Emergency Communications (EMTEL); European Public Warning System (EU-ALERT) using the Cell Broadcast Service (p.8):
5 EU-Alert capabilities 5.1 Language The need to support Public Warning Messages in various languages is necessary for the European Public Warning System because there are many European countries that share borders where there is a frequent and significant movement of mobile subscribers across those borders, i.e. a high instance of international roaming. Emergency messages should be sent out to users in their own language but when not practicable, then in the language of the message originator. It is impractical to determine the language of the user and so messages shall be sent out in the native language of the country originating the message and subject to national requirements, in any other language or languages that the originator chooses. A CBS structure is required to accommodate the requirement to broadcast messages in multiple languages virtually simultaneously in order not to disadvantage any recipient of a message in a particular language. ETSI TS 123 041 [1] contains an assignment of Message Identifiers for EU-Alert messages in the local language, which is the same range as for CMAS messages in English. This range of Message Identifiers shall be used when the national requirements demand that the UE receive and display the EU-Alert messages in local languages unconditionally.

It collects operational and organizational requirements as a basis for a common notification service, including targeting of the area to be notified. Although many of the requirements relate to national public policies and regulations, there are a number of service and technical aspects which are better dealt with on the European level to ensure harmonized access and services over Europe and service effectiveness through increased user awareness by using standardized solutions. 3GPP WG SA1 conducted a study for requirements for PWS in ETSI TR 122 968 [i.2], where the EMTEL specification ETSI TS 102 182 [3], requirements from Japan for ETWS and requirements from the USA for CMAS were used as input. From this study, 3GPP Working Group SA1 delivered a specification for PWS Requirements in ETSI TS 122 268 [2] which covers PWS in general, where ETWS, WEA/CMAS, EU-Alert and KPAS are regional adaptations of PWS. data.summary: The single Portuguese phone text fits on one GSM-7 page, well under the 15-page cell broadcast limit, and the profile requires no other languages. However, the text reads 'Defesa Civil: misantropi4', which looks garbled or placeholder. It names neither a hazard nor a protective action, so a handset recipient on the first (and only) page would not know what is happening or what to do.

objections.issue: The first and only page has no recognisable hazard and no protective action. After the sender label, the content is a meaningless token ('misantropi4'), so recipients cannot tell what the threat is or what to do.
objections.fix: Replace the text with a Portuguese message whose first page names the hazard, the affected area and the action to take. Example form: 'Defesa Civil: <perigo> em <área>. <ação>.' Keep it GSM-7 and within the page limit.

evidence.quote: help communities communicate clearly and effectively about imminent threats

no_basis.concern: No clause shown explicitly states that the first cell broadcast page must carry the hazard and the action. The objection rests mainly on the phone text itself.
